content: 1. The importation of a product is not permitted unless the applicant explicitly authorizes a secondary operator to import the product. In other countries, once a pesticide is registered, anyone can apply for an import or distribution permit for that product. 2. Pesticide legislation should specify that the registration of a pesticide is valid only for a defined period. After this period, the registration automatically expires unless the product is re-registered. Re-registration must be requested by the registration holder if they wish to keep the product on the market. 3. Re-registration typically requires a new application and involves a reassessment to determine whether the conditions that justified the initial registration remain valid. This reassessment places particular emphasis on new information regarding the product's efficacy, risks, and the availability of less hazardous alternatives. 4. If the registration expires without renewal through re-registration, the registration is canceled, and the product can no longer be distributed or used. 5. Legislation should mandate that the registration holder notify the registration authority of any changes to the data submitted with the initial registration application. The law should also define the implications of different types of changes. 6. If the product itself, its composition, active ingredient, or formulation is altered, a new registration application should be required, including a new risk assessment. Changes in packaging, labeling, or usage generally require a new risk-based assessment before the registration certificate can be amended. 7. Minor changes, such as updates to the applicant's contact details, may only require notification to the registration authority. 8. The law should allow the registration authority to review a registration or provisional registration at any time in light of new information about health or environmental effects associated with the pesticide's use. This information may come from international conventions, additional testing, poisoning cases, environmental damage, resistance, phytotoxicity, or regulatory actions in other countries. 9. The registration authority should have the power to impose additional conditions on the manufacture, handling, and application of a pesticide or to revoke the registration if continued use poses an unacceptable risk. Registration should also be revoked if fraudulent information was provided in the application. 10. The registration authority should maintain a register of pesticides containing basic information on all registered products, including brand name, common name, concentration, formulation, uses, and the applicant's name and address. This list should be publicly accessible and easy to consult. 11. A dossier for each registered pesticide should be maintained, containing detailed information on the product's composition, co-formulants, hazards, test reports, and other necessary data. In some countries, certain elements of this information may be protected by industrial property rights or confidentiality. 12. Confidential information, such as manufacturing processes, inert additives, and sensitive business data, should be protected. However, this protection must be balanced with stakeholders' right to access information relevant to health and environmental transparency. 13. Information about co-formulants that may pose additional health or environmental risks should be publicly accessible. Legislation should clearly define which information is public and which is confidential, particularly concerning intellectual property rights. 14. The law should ensure that imported pesticides are inspected at the port of entry to verify their quality, packaging, and labeling. Customs departments play a critical role in preventing the importation of unregistered or improperly packaged pesticides. 15. In cases of non-compliance, the law should provide clear instructions on actions to be taken, such as returning the consignment to the sender. Care should be taken to avoid confiscation of illegally imported pesticides in countries lacking facilities for environmentally sound disposal of hazardous waste. 16. Exported pesticides must meet the standards required by the importing country. Under WTO agreements, equal standards should apply to both imported and domestically manufactured products. 17. The Rotterdam Convention requires parties to implement the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure for pesticides listed in Annex III. This ensures that importing parties are informed and can decide whether to accept future shipments of specific chemicals. 18. Exporting parties must comply with the import decisions of importing parties within six months of being informed by the Convention's secretariat. Additionally, parties exporting banned or severely restricted chemicals must provide an export notification to the importing party. 19. The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants and the Basel Convention on hazardous wastes also contain provisions affecting the import and export of pesticides. These conventions regulate the movement of hazardous substances to ensure environmentally sound disposal or permitted use. 20. Pesticide laws typically require all individuals or businesses involved in manufacturing, importing, formulating, packaging, distributing, or selling pesticides to hold a valid license. Specialized applicators, such as aerial sprayers, may also require licensing. 21. Licensing ensures regulatory control over specific activities or products and allows governments to maintain oversight of pesticide production, importation, and distribution. It also facilitates communication with license holders and ensures compliance with legal requirements. 22. Licensing differs from registration in its purpose and scope. While registration involves a comprehensive review of a product's safety and efficacy, licensing focuses on ensuring that operators meet the necessary legal and technical requirements to handle pesticides responsibly.
